title: No to typing: friction is learning
author: Lead Time
summary: The author recalls a formative teaching moment in Shanghai in 2011, when a class of strong IB Business students who had spent 18 months typing all their notes on 1:1 laptops emerged from mock exams unable to sustain the handwriting speed the paper exam demanded -- their 'handwriting stamina had gone,' even though they knew the content cold. Returning to that memory 15 years later, the author connects it to research on note-taking: Mueller and Oppenheimer's widely-cited 2014 finding that handwritten notes produced better conceptual understanding than typed notes (while flagging that replication attempts have been far less decisive), and Robert and Elizabeth Bjork's concept of 'desirable difficulties' -- friction that makes performance feel harder in the short term while improving long-term retention. The argument's real target isn't the device but the cognitive task: typing lets students transcribe near-verbatim without selecting or processing information, while handwriting's slowness forces decisions about what matters, and it's the deciding, not the pen, that produces 'memory is the residue of thought.' The piece's sharpest turn is toward AI: where laptops let students transcribe faster than they could write, today's tools can remove the need to write, summarize, or even think about a lecture at all, so the practical question for teachers becomes designing tasks that force the same cognitive work regardless of which tool is in a student's hand.
points: Anchors the argument in a vivid classroom anecdote: after 18 months of laptop note-taking, strong IB students physically could not sustain handwriting speed in a paper exam and failed to finish, despite knowing the content.

Cites Mueller and Oppenheimer's 2014 study on handwritten vs. typed notes while explicitly flagging that later replication attempts produced 'much less decisive results' -- a rare example of an ed-writer citing research honestly rather than overselling a single famous study.

Introduces the Bjorks' 'desirable difficulties' concept to reframe why removing friction isn't always good pedagogy: retrieval, selection, and organizing effort are often 'the work' of learning, not a design flaw to eliminate.

Extends the argument to generative AI directly, noting that where laptops let students transcribe faster than they could think, AI tools can remove the need to select, summarize, or process information at all.
quotes: They knew the content. They knew how to answer the questions. But after around 18 months doing almost everything on laptops, many of them could no longer sustain handwriting at the speed the examination demanded.

Mueller and Oppenheimer's well-known 2014 study found that students taking notes by hand performed better on conceptual questions than students using laptops. Laptop users recorded more words and were more likely to reproduce lectures verbatim.
There is good reason to be cautious here. Subsequent attempts to replicate the original findings have produced much less decisive results.

Robert Bjork and Elizabeth Bjork describe the idea of desirable difficulties: conditions that can make performance feel harder in the short term while improving learning and retention over the longer term.
If I can type every word you say, I can capture without selecting. If I cannot keep up, I have to decide. And it's the deciding that requires thinking.
Every one of those tools can be useful. But each also removes a potential point at which the learner might previously have had to select, retrieve, organise, summarise or generate.
